title: Computational threshold for tensor PCA
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <(k- 2)/4\), and rational \(c\in (0,1)\), is the following impossibility statement true? No uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm, given the finite-precision observation of \(Y=n^{k/4- \varepsilon}v^{\otimes k}+Z\) specified below, achieves |\(\langle u,v\rangle |\ge c\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large dimension n, where v is uniform on the unit sphere in \(R^{n}\) and the \(n^{k}\) ordered entries of Z are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables.
definitions: The experiment draws v, Z and the algorithm’s random bits independently. For an ordered tuple \((i_{1},\ldots ,i_{k})\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}^{k}\), the signal entry is \(n^{k/4- \varepsilon}v_{i_{1}}\cdots v_{i_{k}}\). Noise is not pre-symmetrized and each entry has variance one. To give polynomial time a precise bit-model meaning, for \(n\ge 2\) set \(b=\lceil 10k \log _{2}n\rceil\) and \(Q_{b}(x)=2^{- b}\lfloor 2^{b} \max (- 2^{b},\min (x,2^{b}))\rfloor\). The input consists of n and all entries \(Q_{b}(Y_{i_{1},\ldots ,i_{k}})\), represented as signed dyadic rationals with \(O(\log  n)\) bits each. This fixed rounding convention is an explicit finite-precision version of the usual Gaussian-model question. An algorithm may depend on the fixed constants \(k, \varepsilon\) and c, but is one probabilistic Turing machine for all n, with worst-case running time polynomial in n on every input and random tape. For fixed k this is polynomial in the input size. It outputs a nonzero rational vector w, interpreted as the unit vector \(u=w/\Vert w\Vert _{2}\); zero or invalid outputs fail. Success is the event |\(\langle w,v\rangle |\ge c\Vert w\Vert _{2}\). The algorithm receives no side information about v, informative initial vector, or additional independent observations. The probability averages over the spike, noise and internal randomness. Absolute correlation makes the target invariant under the unavoidable sign ambiguity when k is even.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed \((k,\varepsilon ,c)\) in the stated ranges, each such polynomial-time algorithm has success probability below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large n; or refute this by giving one fixed triple and one algorithm that succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\) for all sufficiently large n. Proving failure only for low-degree polynomials, a chosen iterative method, or a different spike prior does not prove the full assertion. An improvement by logarithmic factors at \(n^{k/4}\) does not supply the fixed power saving \(n^{\varepsilon}\) requested here.
why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.

importance.reason: A central average-case inference problem linking tensor algorithms, statistical thresholds, low-degree methods and computational hardness.

progress.text: Montanari–Richard introduce and analyze the spiked tensor model, exhibiting a gap between information-theoretic recovery and the analyzed polynomial-time methods.
Kunisky–Moore–Wein prove spherical-prior low-degree detection thresholds and odd-order reconstruction lower bounds with the predicted dependence on degree.
Wu–Zhou sharpen the analysis and stopping rule for randomly initialized power iteration; its threshold improves by a polylogarithmic factor.
Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang improve stochastic-gradient guarantees in a multiple-observation model; the even-order bound reaches the familiar conjectured computational scale.
Fu–Sohn establish low-degree estimation bounds for independent-coordinate priors, with the predicted degree–signal dependence and an additional technical restriction on degree.

status_note: The May 2026 low-degree paper retains the conjectured gap for unrestricted algorithms and distinguishes spherical from independent-coordinate priors. The 2024 power-iteration and October 2025 stochastic-gradient improvements concern particular methods and do not provide a fixed-power improvement below \(n^{k/4}\). No full resolution found through 11 September 2026. The card explicitly fixes a finite-precision bit model; restricted lower bounds in the standard unrounded model are evidence, not a proof for all algorithms here.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order \(\sqrt{n}\). Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order \(\sqrt{n}\) here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around \(n^{k/4}\), up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from \(\sqrt{n}\). The interval for \(\varepsilon\) deliberately places our target strictly between them: \(\lambda /\sqrt{n}=n^{(k- 2)/4- \varepsilon}\) grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and \(\varepsilon =1/8\), the observation contains \(n^{4}\) noisy numbers and signal strength \(n^{7/8}\). The statistical scale is \(n^{1/2}\), and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all \(n^{4}\) entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as \(vv^{T}\) and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Some recent algorithmic improvements resolve narrower conjectures. Wu and Zhou lower the threshold for randomly initialized power iteration by a polylogarithmic factor. Ding, Gu, Liu and Fang obtain improved guarantees for an overparameterized stochastic-gradient method using multiple independent observations. For even order, their stated sample-signal condition reaches the familiar \(n^{k/4}\) scale after averaging the observations. Neither result supplies the fixed-power improvement below that scale demanded here.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most \(n^{k/2}2^{- b}\), an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.

upgraded_from.title: The computational threshold for dense tensor PCA

sentences: Dense tensor PCA observes a hidden rank-one tensor corrupted by independent Gaussian noise.
The conjecture says that below a specified signal scale, no polynomial-time algorithm can recover a vector with constant correlation to the hidden direction.
It asks about unrestricted computation rather than the performance of a particular spectral, gradient, or low-degree method.
Resolving the threshold would clarify a prominent proposed gap between statistical recoverability and computational feasibility.

The saved formulation fixes finite precision, unit-sphere normalization, one observation, and independent ordered noise entries, so results using different normalizations or extra samples require careful conversion.
